papers.title: Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Racial Discrimination: A Field Experiment
takeaways: The authors sent about 15,000 fake online job applications to employers in New Jersey and New York City, before and after Ban-the-Box laws. They randomly varied whether the name sounded Black or white and whether the applicant had a felony record.
Criminal records do hold people back. Employers who asked about records were 63% more likely to call back applicants without one.
But removing the question made the racial gap much bigger. At those employers, white applicants' callback advantage over Black applicants rose from 7% to 43%.
The authors' explanation: without record information, employers fall back on exaggerated beliefs about racial differences in conviction rates.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 2 — discrimination in hiring.

papers.title: The Effect of Job Loss and Unemployment Insurance on Crime in Brazil
papers.authors: Diogo G. C. Britto, Paolo Pinotti & Breno Sampaio
takeaways: The data link job histories, criminal records, and welfare records for every male worker in Brazil from 2009 to 2017.
Losing a job in a mass layoff raises the chance of committing a crime by 23% on average. The effect is slightly smaller for sons living in the same household.
Using causal forests (a machine-learning method), the authors find the effect comes entirely from young workers and those with short job tenure. Education and income make no difference.
Comparing workers just above and below the cutoff for unemployment benefits shows that benefits fully cancel out the rise in crime. The rise returns as soon as benefits run out.
That timing points to money shortages and stress as the cause, not extra free time.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 2 — job loss and crime.

papers.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco
papers.authors: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade & Franklin Qian
takeaways: A 1994 law put some San Francisco rentals under rent control but not others, creating a natural experiment. Data on where people moved let the authors follow both tenants and landlords.
Covered tenants were 20% less likely to move, and fewer were pushed out of the city. The policy helped people who already had a lease.
Landlords of covered buildings cut their rental units by 15%, by selling to owner-occupiers or redeveloping.
With fewer rentals on the market, rents rose across the city. The policy likely helped current tenants but hurt future renters.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 3 — housing: rent control.

papers.title: Can You Move to Opportunity? Evidence from the Great Migration
takeaways: Moving to a better place can help children. This paper asks what happens when so many people move that the destination itself changes.
Shifts in the racial makeup of northern US cities during the Great Migration (1940 to 1970) reduced the benefits of growing up there for Black families.
This explains 27% of the region's racial gap in upward mobility today.
To isolate the effect, the authors predict where migrants went from where earlier Black migrants (before 1940) had settled and how many people were expected to leave each southern county.
The cause is the places, not the kind of families who moved. The proposed channels are lasting segregation and more crime and policing.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 3 — housing: moving to opportunity.

papers.title: "High" Achievers? Cannabis Access and Academic Performance
takeaways: Maastricht banned some nationalities from its licensed cannabis shops. This is about as close to randomly assigning legal cannabis access as policy gets.
The authors compare course grades of Maastricht University students who lost access with those who did not, before and during the ban.
Students who lost legal access did much better. Gains were largest for younger students, and stronger for women and low performers.

Gains were bigger in math-heavy courses, and students reported understanding the material better rather than studying more. That suggests cannabis affects how well students think, not just how they spend their time.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 4 — drug policy. Marie is one of the course lecturers.

papers.title: The Power of Abortion Policy: Reexamining the Effects of Young Women's Access to Reproductive Control
takeaways: Earlier research often lumped together two policies: access to the birth control pill and access to abortion. This paper separates them.
Changes in sexual behavior fit the idea that the pill drove the sexual revolution.
But neither those trends nor the main estimates show the pill changing when women married or had children.
Abortion access is what holds up. It let many women delay marriage and motherhood.
A good example of a famous finding that holds up for behavior but had credited the wrong policy.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 4 — access to birth control. This is the paper Jun Lim and I presented.

papers.title: What Happens to Workers at Firms that Automate?
papers.authors: James Bessen, Maarten Goos, Anna Salomons & Wiljan van den Berge
takeaways: Dutch data record how much each private firm actually spends on outside automation services. Earlier studies had to guess automation from robot imports or electricity use.
Automation spending comes in sudden spikes. The authors treat each spike as the moment a firm automates and compare workers before and after.
After a firm automates, its existing workers are more likely to leave.
Workers who leave lose 9% of one year's earnings in total over five years, mostly from days without work. Losses are bigger at smaller firms and for older and middle-educated workers.
Spending on computers causes no such losses, which shows the result is about automation specifically.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 5 — automation: winners and losers.

papers.title: The Abolition of Immigration Restrictions and the Performance of Firms and Workers: Evidence from Switzerland
papers.authors: Andreas Beerli, Jan Ruffner, Michael Siegenthaler & Giovanni Peri
takeaways: A reform let European cross-border workers work freely in Switzerland. It mattered more in regions near the border, which lets the authors compare regions.
Foreign employment rose a lot.
Although the new cross-border workers were highly educated, wages of highly educated native workers went up.
The reason is that demand for skills rose at the same time. Skill-intensive firms grew and became more productive and innovative, and new firms arrived, opening manager jobs for natives.
The effects were concentrated in firms that reported skill shortages before the reform, which supports this explanation.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 5 — migration and the labour market.

papers.title: Eclipse of Rent-Sharing: The Effects of Managers' Business Education on Wages and the Labor Share in the US and Denmark
papers.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Alex He & Daniel le Maire
takeaways: Managers with a business degree lower their workers' pay. Within five years, wages fall 6% and workers' share of firm income falls 5 percentage points in the US. In Denmark, the drops are 3% and 3 points.
Firms that hire these managers were not already on different paths, and they gain no extra output, investment, or jobs. So business managers are not simply running leaner, more productive firms.
To show cause and effect, the authors use manager retirements and deaths, plus how the hiring practice spread within industries, regions, and firm sizes.
When export demand rises for reasons outside the firm, managers without a business degree share the gains with workers. Business-degree managers do not.
In Denmark, role models who shape what students choose to study help separate what business school teaches from the kind of people who choose it.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 6 — managers and rent sharing. The syllabus cites this as Acemoglu et al. (2025), but as of September 2026 it is still unpublished: le Maire's homepage lists it under working papers, conditionally accepted at the American Economic Review. Cite the NBER working paper until that lands.

papers.title: Fanning the Flames of Hate: Social Media and Hate Crime
papers.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association, 19(4)
takeaways: Anti-refugee posts on Facebook predict attacks on refugees, but only in German towns where more people use social media. What matters is not the sentiment alone but how widely it can spread.
To show cause and effect, the authors use major Facebook and internet outages that happen for unrelated reasons.
Right-wing social media posts cover a narrower range of topics and use more loaded language than news reports, consistent with echo chambers.
The claim is that social media spreads extreme views and so fuels violent crime. It does not create the hostility in the first place.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 7 — hate speech and violence.
